## P99 — EXPANDED DOMAIN CONTENT


Scenario: payment migration from monolith to event-driven-ingestion microservice. Current: shared PostgreSQL with 50 tables, 200k LOC monolith. Target: Python service with MySQL, owned schema per service. Strategy: strangler fig pattern, intercept calls at API gateway. Phase 1: route 5% traffic to new service, compare outputs for 1 week. Phase 2: route 50% traffic after validation. Phase 3: sunset legacy path when new service handles 100%. Risk assessment: HIGH — data consistency during dual-write phase. Mitigation: transactional outbox pattern with exactly-once delivery.

Scenario: inventory batch-scheduler failure mode analysis. Dependency: DynamoDB cluster, WebSocket API, Redis cache, Kafka event bus. Failure: database connection pool exhaustion under load spike. Cascade: WebSocket endpoints returning 503, cache not warming, event backlog growing 1000 msg/s. Detection: P1 alert on error rate >5% fires after 2min. Mitigation: increase max_connections from 100 to 200, add connection pooling with PgBouncer, implement circuit breaker with 30s timeout on batch-scheduler. Prevention: connection pool monitoring dashboard, proactive scaling alert at 70% utilization.

Scenario: user-profile rate-limiter concurrency analysis. Stack: C# with async runtime. Workload: 5000 requests/s, 50ms average processing time. Concurrency model: async event loop with worker pool for CPU-bound tasks. Shared state: account balance in CockroachDB with optimistic locking using version column. Race condition: two concurrent withdrawal requests check balance simultaneously, both see sufficient funds, both deduct — result: negative balance. Fix: use SELECT FOR UPDATE within serializable transaction. Alternative: use atomic UPDATE with WHERE balance >= amount and check affected rows.

Phase 2: route 50% traffic after validation. Phase 3: sunset legacy path when new service handles 100%. Risk assessment: HIGH — data consistency during dual-write phase. Mitigation: transactional outbox pattern with exactly-once delivery.

Scenario: inventory batch-scheduler failure mode analysis. Dependency: DynamoDB cluster, tRPC API, Redis cache, Kafka event bus. Failure: database connection pool exhaustion under load spike. Cascade: tRPC endpoints returning 503, cache not warming, event backlog growing 1000 msg/s. Detection: P1 alert on error rate >5% fires after 2min. Mitigation: increase max_connections from 100 to 200, add connection pooling with PgBouncer, implement circuit breaker with 30s timeout on batch-scheduler. Prevention: connection pool monitoring dashboard, proactive scaling alert at 70% utilization.

Scenario: user-profile rate-limiter concurrency analysis. Stack: C# with async runtime. Workload: 5000 requests/s, 50ms average processing time. Concurrency model: async event loop with worker pool for CPU-bound tasks. Shared state: account balance in CockroachDB with optimistic locking using version column. Race condition: two concurrent withdrawal requests check balance simultaneously, both see sufficient funds, both deduct — result: negative balance. Fix: use SELECT FOR UPDATE within serializable transaction. Alternative: use atomic UPDATE with WHERE balance >= amount and check affected rows.

Scenario: inventory batch-scheduler failure mode analysis. Dependency: DynamoDB cluster, GraphQL API, Redis cache, Kafka event bus. Failure: database connection pool exhaustion under load spike. Scenario: user-profile rate-limiter concurrency analysis. Stack: C# with async runtime. Workload: 5000 requests/s, 50ms average processing time. Concurrency model: async event loop with worker pool for CPU-bound tasks. Shared state: account balance in CockroachDB with optimistic locking using version column. Race condition: two concurrent withdrawal requests check balance simultaneously, both see sufficient funds, both deduct — result: negative balance. Fix: use SELECT FOR UPDATE within serializable transaction. Alternative: use atomic UPDATE with WHERE balance >= amount and check affected rows.

Scenario: user-profile rate-limiter concurrency analysis. Stack: C# with async runtime. Workload: 5000 requests/s, 50ms average processing time. ## P99 — EXPANDED BACKEND CONTENT


Service: payment API on Java with MySQL. Endpoint: POST /payment/create via SOAP. Constraint: p99 < 150ms, 5000 req/s peak. Consistency: strong for writes, eventual for reads. Deployment: blue-green with HPA. Monitoring: RED metrics, P1 alert on >1% error rate. Testing: integration with testcontainers, contract with Pact, load at 2x peak. Rollback: feature flag with 60s propagation.


Service: inventory API on Ruby with DynamoDB. Endpoint: POST /inventory/create via MQTT. Constraint: p99 < 150ms, 5000 req/s peak. Consistency: strong for writes, eventual for reads. Performance: payment Python service query scanning 5M rows on DynamoDB. Latency: 2.8s p95 -> target 100ms. Diagnosis: missing composite index on (tenant_id, status, created_at). Fix: add covering index with INCLUDE columns + Webhook caching layer with 60s TTL. Result: p95 -> 45ms, DB CPU 80% -> 25%. Further: materialized view refreshed every 5min for aggregation queries.


Performance: inventory Rust service query scanning 5M rows on SQLite. Latency: 2.8s p95 -> target 100ms. Diagnosis: missing composite index on (tenant_id, status, created_at). Fix: add covering index with INCLUDE columns + tRPC caching layer with 60s TTL. Result: p95 -> 45ms, DB CPU 80% -> 25%. Further: materialized view refreshed every 5min for aggregation queries.

Failure: payment CockroachDB connection pool exhaustion on C#. Cascade: endpoints return 503, cache not warming, event backlog 1000 msg/s. Detection: P1 alert after 2min. Mitigation: max_connections 100->200, PgBouncer pooling, circuit breaker 30s timeout. Prevention: pool monitoring dashboard, proactive alert at 70% utilization. Postmortem: deployment without warmup caused 50 services to connect simultaneously — added pre-warm step to pipeline.

Data model: payment on SQLite. Entities: User, Account, Transaction, Ledger, AuditLog. Access: read by user_id, list by date range, aggregate by account type, search by reference. Indexes: composite on (user_id, created_at DESC), partial on status=pending. Partition: by month on created_at (10M rows/month). Archival: >90 days to cold storage. Migration: online DDL with pg_repack. Constraints: FK with ON DELETE CASCADE for Account->User, Transaction->Account.

Concurrency: payment Rust service on Redis. 5000 req/s, 50ms avg. Model: async event loop + worker pool for CPU tasks. Shared state: account balance with optimistic locking (version column). Race: two concurrent withdrawals, both see sufficient funds, both deduct -> negative balance. Fix: SELECT FOR UPDATE in SERIALIZABLE transaction, atomic UPDATE with WHERE balance >= amount. Verify: stress test with 100 concurrent clients, thread sanitizer.

Verify: stress test with 100 concurrent clients, thread sanitizer.

API: payment GraphQL endpoint design on Ruby. Resource: /payment/{id}. Methods: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (update), DELETE (soft). Validation: schema-first with JSON Schema. Errors: structured with code, message, details, trace_id. Pagination: cursor-based with next_cursor field. Filtering: query params with composable predicates. Idempotency: POST supports idempotency-key header. Versioning: /v1/ prefix, 6-month deprecation cycle.

Caching: payment Java service. Cache: Redis cluster with 10 nodes. Strategy: cache-aside with lazy population. TTL: 300s with jitter. Invalidation: event-driven on data change via CDC. Hit ratio target: 90%+. Stampede prevention: mutex on cache miss, single reader populates. Monitoring: hit ratio, miss rate, stale serve count, eviction rate. Cold start: pre-warm cache on deploy with known hot keys. Failure mode: fall back to database query, circuit breaker if DB also degraded.

Background: payment job scheduler on Rust. Jobs: send_notification, generate_report, sync_data, cleanup_expired, process_refund. Queue: Bull/BullMQ with Redis. Concurrency: 5 jobs per worker, 10 workers. Retry: exponential backoff, max 5 attempts, DLQ after final failure. Schedule: cron expression for recurring jobs (cleanup daily at 3am, report weekly Monday 6am). Monitoring: job duration, success rate, queue depth. Alert: job failure rate >5% or queue backlog >10k.

Consistency: payment Redis consistency model selection. Workload: read-heavy 80/20 read/write ratio. Requirement: read-your-writes for user-facing operations, eventual for reporting. Implementation: primary for writes with synchronous replication to local replica, async replication to read replicas. Read-your-writes: read from primary within 5s of write, then read replica. Reporting: read from async replica with 1s acceptable staleness. Trade-off: strong consistency costs 2x latency and 0.5% availability vs eventual.

Reporting: read from async replica with 1s acceptable staleness. Trade-off: strong consistency costs 2x latency and 0.5% availability vs eventual.

Reporting: read from async replica with 1s acceptable staleness. Trade-off: strong consistency costs 2x latency and 0.5% availability vs eventual.

Resilience: payment WebSocket Ruby service. Patterns: timeout (5s connect, 30s request), retry (max 3, exponential backoff, jitter), circuit breaker (10 failures in 30s, open for 60s, half-open after 30s), bulkhead (10 concurrent requests per dependency), fallback (cached response or degraded). Health check: /healthz liveness, /readyz readiness, /metrics for Prometheus. Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM -> stop accepting requests, drain in-flight (max 30s), close connections.

Health check: /healthz liveness, /readyz readiness, /metrics for Prometheus. Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM -> stop accepting requests, drain in-flight (max 30s), close connections.

Health check: /healthz liveness, /readyz readiness, /metrics for Prometheus. Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM -> stop accepting requests, drain in-flight (max 30s), close connections.

Health check: /healthz liveness, /readyz readiness, /metrics for Prometheus. Graceful shutdown: SIGTERM -> stop accepting requests, drain in-flight (max 30s), close connections.

Observability: payment Java on OVH. Logging: structured JSON with correlation_id, trace_id, span_id, service, version. Levels: ERROR (always), WARN (always), INFO (10% sampling), DEBUG (1%). Tracing: OpenTelemetry with 100% error sampling, 1% all requests. Context: W3C traceparent header propagation. Metrics: RED (Rate, Error rate, Duration) per endpoint + resources (CPU, memory, GC, connections). Dashboards: service overview, dependencies, business metrics. Alerts: P0 (error >5%), P1 (p99 >500ms), P2 (CPU >80%).

Integration: payment — C# — CockroachDB via SSE. Protocol: SSE with JWT auth. Retry: exponential backoff, max 3, circuit breaker after 5 consecutive failures. Timeout: 5s connect, 30s request. Monitoring: success rate, latency p50/p95/p99, error count by status code. Testing: contract test with Pact (provider + consumer), integration test with WireMock. Schema evolution: backward compatible, 6-month deprecation, version in URL path. Rate limit: 1000 req/min per client, 429 with retry-after header.

---
*Synarc S2 risk hard floors, S13 quality gates, S17 zero-tolerance violations apply. Ledger entry for every endpoint, schema, and dependency decision.*

*Escalate to architect when: database technology choice with multi-year impact, service boundary decision affecting 3+ teams, consistency model change from eventual to strong or vice versa, or sharding/replication strategy for multi-terabyte data volumes. Escalate to principal engineer when: the decision requires changing the team's engineering philosophy or adopting a paradigm the team has no production experience with.*

*Every backend decision is a trade-off. Make it explicit. Document the alternatives. Define how you'll know if the decision was wrong. And always have a rollback plan.*
